3.text: especially those not yet fully grown, when desiring to die, destroy their life

4.text: with their own hands, while those who are older more frequently ask to be

5.text: killed. I know some cases of boys and girls who were not yet twenty, and

6.text: who killed themselves from spite, shame, or sorrow.¹ Not one of them could

10.text: An additional source for this inclination for voluntary death is the idea

11.text: that death by violence is preferable to death by disease or old age. Even

12.text: the term which is used for “voluntary death” has some connection with this

13.text: idea. It is called vêrêˊtɪrg̣ɪn (“single fight”). A man who feels a desire to

14.text: die a voluntary death sometimes even says, “Let us have a single fight”

15.text: (Mɪnmarauˊmɪk), or “Since like a wild reindeer I became for thee” (Čeˊñet-

16.text: ɪm ɪlveˊnu ineˊlhɪiᵋ); and this is understood as a request to be killed. Another

17.text: expression is used chiefly in folk-tales: “Since I became for thee like thy

18.text: quarry” (Čeˊñet-ɪm g̣ɪˊnnɪku ineˊlhɪiᵋ), or, more directly, “Like thy quarry treat

19.text: me” (G̣ɪˊnniku qineˊlhɪiᵋ). These formulas are used by warriors when they are

20.text: vanquished by an adversary and do not want to outlive their defeat. The

21.text: meaning is, “Give me a mortal stroke, since I have become for you as a

22.text: game-animal.” The same formula is sometimes used in real life by those

23.text: desiring voluntary death. The Chukchee explained the motive to me, saying,

24.text: “We do not want to die through keˊlet. We want to die a violent death,

25.text: to die fighting, as if we were fighting with the Russians.” The Russians were

26.text: singled out probably for my own benefit. Death by disease, as has been

27.text: explained before, is ascribed to the wiles of the keˊlet.² The tendency to

28.text: desire voluntary death is more or less hereditary in some Chukchee families,

29.text: not so much as a duty, as rather a fate which passes from father to son.

30.text: In a detailed description of a case of voluntary death, which I noted down

31.text: from the words of natives, it is said, “Since his father died this way, he

32.text: wanted to imitate him.” The father was stabbed with a knife; but, when

33.text: death did not come immediately, he requested that he be strangled with a

34.text: rope, which was done accordingly. The son also was stabbed, but the stroke

35.text: was not mortal. So he went still further in imitating his father, and also

36.text: requested that he might die by strangulation, which was immediately executed.

37.text: Aiñanwaˊt, whose name has been mentioned several times, told me that

38.text: his father and elder brother died this way, and that he himself felt an inclination

39.text: to end his life in the same manner, though it is by no means obligatory for

40.text: a son to follow the example of his father. One of his brothers died a natural

41.text: death, and so did not continue the tradition.
